title: Kurzgesagt-Style What If Explainer
author: finnardley
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: one topic as a "what if" question (default: "What if the Sun vanished?"), the length (default 30 seconds), and whether I have an ElevenLabs key (if not, use a free local voice).
</inputs>

<direction>
A Kurzgesagt-style animated explainer at 1920x1080, 30fps, drawn entirely in code: one 2D canvas plus one WebGL canvas for planets.
Space: a vertical gradient #081d2c to #102348, five huge parallax nebula blobs (teal rgb 24,150,160 at 20%, blue 40,95,195 at 16%, coral 220,95,110 at 10%, indigo 60,70,175 at 15%), three star layers at parallax depths .12/.35/.6 that twinkle, 40% of the near stars drawn as 4-point sparkles.
The Sun: radius 300px, half off the left edge. A radial gradient #fff7dc to #ffc857 to #ff8f4a with an offset highlight, additive halo rings at 1.23/1.48/1.76/2.1x the radius, 18 faint rotating ray wedges, 28 drifting glowing granules on its surface.
Earth: an orthographic sphere in a fragment shader, 4x supersampled, from a 2048x1024 map painted from longitude/latitude polygons: land #5fc47a, forest #48ad6b, desert #f5c75f, rainforest #3a9d62, ice #f1f8ff, ocean gradient #4dc7eb to #1a66b8, white capsule clouds. Tilt .26 rad, spin .55 degrees per second. Day/night uses smoothstep(-.12, .24, N·L) with the light direction recomputed from Sun to Earth every frame. Navy night side with ~380 warm city lights, a coral band on the terminator, a cyan rim, ocean specular, an atmosphere halo that is stronger on the lit side.
A small astronaut mascot (~180px) built from rounded rectangles: suit #f3f7fb, orange #ff8f4a boots, a visor gradient #1f5a73 to #0a1c2c with glowing cyan eyes that look at whatever matters, a blinking antenna light, an idle bob, squash and stretch on every pose.
Type: Fredoka 600/700 only. Captions in caps with 3-6px letter spacing in teal #8fd8e6, gold #ffd98a or white, sitting in rounded pills of rgb(6,20,40) at 62%. Every line of text rises 1.3x its own height through a clip on an ease-out-quint.
Finish: a vignette to rgba(4,4,20,.45) and a 6% film grain re-randomized 24 times per second.
Banned: outlines, flares or loops on the Sun's edge, static infographic strips, full stops in on-screen text, text that fades in whole, AI images or AI video, Kurzgesagt's own characters, bird or music.
</direction>

<structure>
30 seconds, every line of narration gets a camera move or a transformation, nothing ever holds still.
Tight on the Sun at 2.25x (0s) → on the word "vanished" it swells 6% for 0.22s, collapses in 0.33s, then a white flash and a shockwave ring (1s) → pull back to 1x revealing Earth still lit and the astronaut staring at the empty spot (1.6-3s) → on "eight" an 8:20 countdown slams in from 1.7x to 1x and starts ticking, a "LAST LIGHT" label rides the edge of the growing dark disc (3.2s) → dive to 2.3x on Earth with light streaks flowing in (5.6s) → on "you" a YOU pin drops (7s) → on "left" a photon lands on the pin with "THIS LIGHT LEFT THE SUN / 8 MIN 20 SEC AGO" (7.5s) → on "play" the pin morphs into a play button, "YOU PRESSED PLAY / 15 SEC AGO" (8.8s) → one pull-back from 2.4x to a 0.3x orbit view, "LAST LIGHT" and "GRAVITY" riding the ring (9.6-12.5s) → on "nothing" a dotted circle at the empty centre (13.4s) → on "hits" the darkness sweeps Earth in 0.7s, city lights pop on, the countdown turns gold at 0:00 (15.8s) → on "black" the background fades almost to black (17.4s) → Jupiter appears, "STILL SHINING FOR 1 HOUR+" (17.9s) → zoom out, a dashed tangent line, "30 KM/S" as Earth flies straight off (20.8s) → a thermometer counts 15 to -70°C while frost grows from the poles (22.8s) → a 0.8s rewind on a separate story clock (24.3s) → sunglasses drop onto the astronaut (25.2s) → a photon tagged "8:20 OLD", then the title (27.7s).
For any other topic, keep the same shape: the event happens on its word, pull back to show scale, dive in to make it personal ("you"), pull back out, the consequence with a live counter, an escalation, a funny beat with the mascot, a callback and the title.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file. Every frame is a pure function of time: window.seek(t) draws frame t. No timers, no CSS animation.
2. Camera moves on easeInOutCubic, zoom is interpolated in log space, every pop is a damped spring (damping .42-.5, frequency 12-16).
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with a designed voice (calm, warm, curious male, late 30s, crisp, light neutral European English), stability .5, similarity .75, generated with timestamps. Without a key, use kokoro-onnx locally and get word times with faster-whisper. Every animation event fires on its word. About 165 words per minute, 0.24s between sentences, a 0.36s beat before the big reveal.
4. The darkness front: any pixel within the front's radius from the Sun turns to night with a 30px soft edge. The front moves at ~47px/s and ramps to 700px/s near Earth.
5. Keep two clocks: ambient time for twinkle, spin and bob, and a separate story clock for events, so a rewind stays consistent.
6. Render with Playwright in headless Edge with the GPU: seek every frame at 30fps and blend 2 subframes (shutter 0.6) for motion blur, then encode with libx264 at CRF 16 for the master and CRF 20 for delivery.
7. Sound: a calm royalty-free space music bed 7dB under the voice, timed so its natural ending lands on the title, swelling 5dB under the title. One downloaded royalty-free sound effect per event kind (collapse, impact, pull-back whoosh, countdown tick, dive, pin tap, photon land, play click, light hit, reveal, frost, rewind), each peak-aligned to its frame and 4-10dB under the voice. Master with gain plus a limiter to -14 LUFS, -2.2dB true peak.
</build>

<gotchas>
Make the WebGL globe canvas at least 2 x radius x zoom x 1.18 pixels or the sphere clips flat in close-ups. Never draw prominences on the Sun's edge, they read as white hooks. Never pad the voice to fit the visuals, tighten the read instead. Speed the darkness front up near Earth or it takes 13 seconds to cross the planet. Show me a contact sheet of every beat before rendering.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me the inputs, write the narration with the beat each word triggers, show it to me, then build and render the video.
</start>

title: Athenaion Procedural Ancient Greek World
author: Leonxlnx
prompt:
Build me a massive, ultra-detailed 3D world in three.js based on the 9 reference images I attached.

Rules:
- Zero external assets. Every mesh, texture, shader and effect has to be generated in code.
- Match the references as closely as possible (aim for 99.9%): composition, scale, materials and
  especially the colors. Cinematic and realistic, not oversaturated, but also not grey or washed out.
- Detail everywhere. Nothing should look copy-pasted or simple. Every building, tree, rock and
  waterfall gets care, and the world has to read as ultra detailed even from far away.
- Waterfalls and water have to look realistic.
- My GPU is weak (integrated Radeon 780M), so keep it efficient and get the quality from offline
  rendering instead.
- Work only inside this project folder.

Process:
- Iterate for as long as it takes (hours or days). Don't stop before it matches the references.
- Render the matching shots as stills and show them to me first. Don't render the video before I approve.
- After I approve: render a cinematic ~1 minute showcase video in 4K at 30fps with slow camera moves
  through the different scenes, no text on screen, impressive from the very first frame, and free
  cinematic background music from the web (credit the artist).

title: Pencil Sharpener Cutter Teardown
author: Nyxera0x
prompt:
You build robotic objects and creatures from a reference image, in three.js, entirely in code.

The look:
- white shells with clearcoat and an environment map
- green as a sparse accent only: tips, rims, edge lines, a bezel, joint rings; never dots sprinkled over a shell
- dark mechanism in 2 levels: big parts (gears, rings, actuators) and about 260 small ones (pistons, hoses, screws, wiring); cut windows into the shells so the dark mass shows
- eyes as glossy black lenses with a thin green bezel and a small pupil
- membranes milky and frosted with thin veins
- every limb has its own pose and segment lengths, never a row of identical parts
- bristles and spikes thin and short: 0.15 to 0.25 of the limb's thickness
- one main set of limbs per creature
- near-white studio, soft floor shadow

The order:
1. Measure the reference first: its main proportions (height, head, jaw or limb length) as shares of its length.
2. Build the object and render one still posed like the reference.
3. Put the reference, your still and an approved still side by side and grade every line of the checklist: yes, partial or no. Grade against the picture, not against what you remember building.
4. Grade one more line every round: at thumbnail size, does it look as dense as the approved still?
5. Measure it: the share of dark pixels in the object's frame, yours against the reference's. Below 0.8 of it is a no.
6. Stop after round 2 and show me. The film waits for my yes.

The camera:
- frame 0 is the front 3/4 hero view, the object big and already moving
- every teardown gets its own side, height and distance, aimed at the part itself, pushing in while it hangs open: an eye in macro, a tail from behind, a back from above, a jaw from below
- the part being opened stays in view; the rest of the object may run off the frame
- smooth paths only: the camera never copies a wing beat or a footstep
- visible wing beats stay slow, 1.5 to 2.5 Hz

When I correct you, the correction goes into this file.

title: Object Strobe Turbo Product Film
author: AmirMushich
prompt:
# OBJECT STROBE: a product film built entirely in code

> Paste this into Claude Code in an empty folder. Replace `[OBJECT]` once, in the line below. Nothing else needs editing.

**OBJECT = [OBJECT]**

You are the technical director and the art director on a 9.6-second vertical loop for Instagram Reels. The hero is
[OBJECT], modelled entirely in code, with no imported models, no stock assets, no logos and no brand names. The film reads as the
output of a machine-vision system diagnosing [OBJECT]:
- the object comes apart and is inspected part by part;
- it goes back together and is pushed past its limit;
- it recovers and settles into one clean hero frame that loops into frame 0 without a seam.

Under the analysis graphics, each part strobes between three passes: **solid** (finished material), **glass**
(dispersive x-ray), and **field** (a simulation plot of the one physical quantity that matters to [OBJECT]).

Work like a studio, not like a demo: every decision below has a reason, and every number on screen has to be true.

---

## 0. How you work

- Work only inside this folder. Keep scripts in `scripts/`, frames in `renders/`, finished files in `deliver/`, notes in `board/`.
- **Every frame is a pure function of its frame number.** No accumulated state and no randomness without a seed. Any frame
  can be re-rendered alone and match its neighbours.
- **One GPU, one render.** Never run two Blender renders at once. Run anything longer than two minutes in the background.
- **Ask before installing software, downloading fonts or spending money.** Say what, from where and how big.
- **Show, then continue.** At each checkpoint (★), build a contact sheet and show it to me before going on:
  - every 6th frame with frame numbers burned in;
  - 100 % crops where detail matters.
- Write a `README.md` as you go: what each script does and the exact commands to reproduce the result.

## 1. Preflight

Check, report in one table, and fix what's missing (after asking):

| Need | Check | If missing |
|---|---|---|
| Blender ≥ 4.2 (needs the *Khronos PBR Neutral* view transform) | `blender --version`. On Windows also try `C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\*\blender.exe`; on macOS `/Applications/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender` | `winget install BlenderFoundation.Blender` / `brew install --cask blender` / the official .tar.xz from blender.org on Linux |
| GPU for Cycles | in Blender's Python: `cycles` prefs `get_devices()`; prefer OPTIX > CUDA > METAL > HIP | CPU works: halve the samples, render at 50 % first, and tell me the time estimate |
| ffmpeg | `ffmpeg -version` | winget `Gyan.FFmpeg` / brew `ffmpeg` / apt `ffmpeg` |
| Python 3.10+ with numpy, opencv-python, pillow | make a local `.venv`, install there, never globally | — |
| Fonts: **Fira Mono** (data) and **Space Grotesk** (tags), both SIL OFL from Google Fonts | look in system or user font folders | ask, then download into `fonts/` and load them by path |

Then render one 540×960 test frame of a cube with the final render settings. Report the device and seconds per frame,
and project the full render time before you build anything.

## 2. Study the object ★

Before modelling, write `board/OBJECT.md`:

1. **Anatomy.** List 25–50 real parts of [OBJECT] with their real names: housings, inner mechanism, fasteners, seals, the
   small parts people never see. Give each one:
   - a group (shell / core / small);
   - a primary material;
   - an **explode vector** (direction and distance along the object's natural assembly axis; large shells travel farthest).
2. **The field.** Pick the ONE physical quantity [OBJECT] truly lives with:
   - heat for an engine part;
   - load for a structure;
   - pressure or flow for a valve or a lung;
   - charge for a battery;
   - vibration for a speaker.

   Name it, give it a unit, a realistic working range and a **limit**. This becomes the story.
3. **The story in four beats**, specific to [OBJECT]:
   - cold, at rest;
   - working, the field rises in a front across the object, from source to far end;
   - **over the limit**, the most extreme frame of the film;
   - recovery, a front running back.
4. **Proportions.** Overall size, key diameters and thicknesses, from real-world references you know. Turn them into one
   constants table that all geometry reads from.

## 3. Build ([OBJECT] in code)

- Model with signed distance functions in numpy and mesh them with surface nets plus a few Newton steps onto the surface
  (crisp edges, no blobby marching-cubes look).
  - Use smooth unions for cast parts, hard booleans for machined ones.
  - Use real threads on fasteners.
  - Use bpy only for assembly and materials.
- Each part is its own object. Each one stores custom properties: `xv` (explode vector), `grp`, `seed`, `tbase` (field
  value 0–1) and `hamp` (field noise amplitude).
- Cache SDF results to disk. Decimate large shells to a sane vertex budget (≈ 3 M vertices total is fine).
- **Hero asset bar:** sculpt-level detail on the parts the camera dwells on. Detail density here buys more than more parts:
  bevels, bosses, ribs, casting seams, machined faces. Do not show a primitive blockout as the hero.
- ★ Look-dev sheet: four configurations (assembled / exploded / core only / close-up) × three passes, rendered at 50 %.

## 4. Look

- **One `Strobe` shader node group** on every part, switched per object through Attribute nodes (OBJECT type): `st` 0 solid,
  1 glass, 2 field.
  - **Glass:** three Glass BSDFs on R, G and B at IOR ≈ 1.47 / 1.51 / 1.57, added together. This is cheap dispersion with
    rainbow edges.
  - **Field:** object-space 4D noise around `tbase`, plus a radial and an axial term, fed through one colour ramp. Emission
    rises with the field value, so hot parts glow and cold ones read as a scan.
- **The field palette has two hues, never a rainbow:**
  - cold: navy → cobalt → ice;
  - an unlit dark band between them;
  - hot: ember → red → orange → near-white.

  No green and no yellow-green: they read as engineering software, not as a film. Define the ramp once (sRGB hex) and use
  the same ramp in the shader, the legend and every inset. In the cold acts, damp the noise so the scan stays blue.
- Studio world: dark ground, two or three hard softboxes. Camera and transmission rays see a pale environment, so the glass
  reads.
- **Film transparent.** Backdrops are composited later, which lets the backdrop change per act.
- Khronos PBR Neutral view transform, exposure −1, 16-bit RGBA PNG.

## 5. Timeline: 288 frames = 6 bars at 150 BPM

One beat is 12 frames and an eighth is 6. **Every cut lands on an eighth.** Act lengths:

| frames | act | configuration | what happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–11 | acquire | assembled, glass ghost, **light** backdrop | the hook: the most beautiful material on frame 0 |
| 12–53 | separation | explode flight | outer parts leave first, small inner parts follow; ease-out, no overshoot |
| 54–89 | inspection | exploded, slow drift | **one continuous shot** that keeps the flight's framing; only materials strobe |
| 90–131 | core lock | close-up on the heart part, outer shells hidden | strip light along the edges, f/1.4 depth of field, three field pulses on beats |
| 132–167 | reassembly | exact reverse order | inner parts seat first, shells close last; the camera follows the shells |
| 168–215 | working | assembled | the field front runs source → far end, on the same curve the graphics draw |
| 216–245 | **limit** | assembled | the extreme of the film: everything in the field pass, an alarm flicker on the beat (2.5 Hz) |
| 246–269 | recovery | assembled | a front runs back; parts return to the solid pass one by one |
| 270–287 | clean | assembled, solid, **light**, **no graphics** | the product alone; framing, drift and rotation run into frame 0 |

- Material states are random only in the diagnostic acts (blocks of 1–4 frames, seeded per part). In the story acts they
  are **deterministic**: a part's pass follows the front.
- **Never intercut configurations that read as different assembly states.** Hold one configuration per act.
- Acts 168–269 are **one continuous camera move**: one slow push and orbit, with no cuts inside the story.

## 6. Camera and motion

- A fixed shot per configuration, with the object's main axis at about −27° on screen and a low, slightly heroic angle.
- **Auto-framing:** project a subsample of the real mesh vertices (not bounding boxes) and fit the lens to a fill target.
  Re-aim at the visual centre, and compute it once per act so repeated shots match.
- Place the subject 70 px above centre: the Reels caption covers the bottom.
- Motion blur from keys at f−0.25, f and f+0.25, computed with that frame's own act, so nothing smears across a cut.
- **Seam math, not eyeballing:** after the render, export each part's projected 2D box per frame. Measure the spread
  (the mean distance of the part centres from their centroid) across every act boundary.
  - A jump over 2 px means a stutter. Fix it in the camera, not in the edit.

## 7. Render ★

- Run `--track` (timeline JSON) and `--track2d` (per-frame part boxes, depth, pass, field value). Then render all
  frames with Cycles at 128 samples, adaptive threshold 0.03, OptiX denoise.
- Frames 0–11 are the hook: render them at 512 samples with threshold 0.01. Grain in the glass at 100 % is not acceptable.
- Render low-res tests of the extremes first (frames 0, 110, 200, 230, 262, 280). Judge the palette on its real backdrop
  before spending the full render.

## 8. The vision layer (graphics in Python)

The graphics are diegetic: they are the machine's own readout, never captions or decoration. Composite them in numpy and
PIL over the raw RGBA frames.

- **Two backdrops only:** light for frames 0–11 and the clean beat, dark for the whole diagnosis.
  - On light, the object casts a soft offset shadow plus a contact shadow.
  - On dark, glowing parts spill a large, warm, blurred glow onto the ground.
  - Add a touch of bloom and chromatic aberration, and one **static** grain texture (grain that changes every frame looks cheap).
- **Blend modes:** white vectors use **Exclusion**, so they invert what is under them; apply this to some elements, not
  all. Over mid-grey, where Exclusion disappears, the ink is picked from the actual pixels under each label.
- **The safe band** (1080×1920): everything readable lives in y 250–1500 and clears the action column on the right
  (x > 930 for y 1000–1500).
- **Type:**
  - Fira Mono 24 / 28 for data, Space Grotesk 34 for part names;
  - Regular weight only (bold reads cheap);
  - 2 px lines, 4 px for the lead line.
  - Labels never overlap: a placed label shifts, or it drops.
- **One lead graphic per act:**
  - acquire: a dashed hull filling in;
  - separation: multi-object tracking with velocity labels and short trails, plus a curved dashed node web;
  - inspection: segmentation boxes on a 30 px grid, with the part names;
  - core lock: crosshair, lock box, a thermal inset and a 1-bit dithered edge inset;
  - reassembly: twelve rays converging on the seat point;
  - working: the front line;
  - limit: the alarm plate;
  - recovery: the recovery front;
  - clean: **nothing**.
- **Glitch with purpose:** datamosh, slice, RGB split or pixel-sort, only *inside* tracked boxes, held for 2–3 frames.
  Never full frame. The bars must sample the part itself, never empty background.
- **Invert slap:** invert, then black and white, then contrast 1.5. Three frames on, three off, three on, at the separation,
  the working start and the limit. **One polarity throughout:** the object as a white silhouette on black, graphics white.
- **Red belongs to the alarm.** It appears only after the limit is truly crossed. Everything else is white.
- **One scale for every number:** each temperature, pressure or load on screen is computed from that part's real field
  value through one function, for example `T = min + (max − min) · v^1.6`.
  - The legend, the insets, the log and the tags all agree.
  - The limit act is the highest reading of the film.
  - Parts the recovery front has passed read as recovered.
  - IDs are consistent everywhere.
- **The log:** a typewriter with a scrambled leading edge, top left. Lines carry live values, not invented ones.

## 9. Sound (synthesised from the timeline, numpy only)

Three layers with roles:
- **mechanics:** impacts, the ejection roll, seat clicks, the lock;
- **machine voice:** the characteristic sound of [OBJECT] at work. Its pitch follows the real state curve from the
  timeline, about two octaves over the working act;
- **data:** blips on log lines, ticks. Keep it about 18 dB under the other layers.

Events:
- a downbeat sound on frame 0;
- the separation as a roll, with three accents on the largest parts;
- near-silence in the inspection;
- three pulses with the core lock;
- a reversed swell into the lock at frame 168;
- one signature double hit for every slap;
- at the limit, a warning on its first beat and the alarm from the frame the limit is crossed;
- a release sound into the recovery;
- one soft air hit when the backdrop turns light.

Render the score twice in a row and keep the second pass, so tails wrap into frame 0. For phones, add harmonics so the
low end survives small speakers, and keep everything under 200 Hz centred. Master with gain plus a limiter to −14 LUFS
integrated and −1.5 dBTP. Check the mono fold-down.

Also write `deliver/cues.csv`: time, frame, bar.beat, event, what. Someone may want to redo the sound by hand.

## 10. Finish and delivery

- Encode with an explicit BT.709 conversion (`scale=out_color_matrix=bt709:out_range=tv`) and write all three colour tags
  into the stream (`h264_metadata` bitstream filter). Untagged files shift gamma on phones.
- Deliver:
  - `*_ig.mp4`: two-pass H.264, 16 Mb/s, AAC 320k;
  - `*_master.mp4`: CRF 15;
  - `*_clean.mp4`: the same film with no graphics and no slaps, for clients;
  - `audio/`: the mix and its stems;
  - `cues.csv`;
  - five 4K stills (hook, close-up, limit, recovery, clean), composited on their own backdrops;
  - a 1080×1920 cover that holds up as a 3:4 grid crop.

## 11. Quality gates (measure them and report the numbers)

1. **Seams:** spread jump ≤ 2 px at every act boundary; the reassembly spread decreases monotonically.
2. **Loop:** the object's bounding box on frames 287 and 0 matches within 2 px. Only the material changes at the loop.
3. **Flashes:** at most 3 full-field luminance flips in any second (aim for far fewer).
4. **Compression:** re-encode at 720p and 2.5 Mb/s, as the platform will, and check that every label is still readable.
5. **Safe band:** draw the Reels UI zones over six frames; no readable element inside them.
6. **Truth:** read every number on six frames aloud against the story. A reading that contradicts the picture is a bug.
7. **Taste:**
   - one hero per frame;
   - nothing static for long;
   - nothing jittering at random;
   - no green;
   - no red before the alarm;
   - no text outside the HUD;
   - no logos.

Finish with a short report: the files, the measured gates, render time and anything you could not verify.

title: Three.js 3D Videos in Under a Minute
author: SebastianHardyAI
prompt:
[OPTIONAL FIRST LINE: Before writing code, show me the scene plan as a table of seconds, camera move and text. Wait for my OK.]

Use Three.js to build a [LENGTH, e.g. 20]-second animated video scene that I can watch right here in the chat as an artifact.

THE WORLD
Subject: [WHAT THE VIDEO IS ABOUT, e.g. a glowing 3D phone showing my booking app]
Setting: [WHERE IT HAPPENS, e.g. a dark glossy studio floor with soft reflections]
Style: [THE LOOK, e.g. clean Apple-style product render, playful toy-like low-poly, or futuristic neon]
Objects in the scene: [LIST THE THINGS, e.g. a phone, three floating app cards, a small coffee cup]

LIGHTING AND COLOUR
Lighting: [e.g. soft key light from the top left, warm rim light from behind, light fog for depth]
Colour palette: background [HEX], main [HEX], accent [HEX], text [HEX]

CAMERA
Camera moves: [e.g. slow push-in, then a smooth half orbit to the right, then rise to a top-down view]
Every camera move eases in and out. No sudden jumps.

TIMELINE
0-3s: [SCENE 1, the opening]
3-8s: [SCENE 2]
8-14s: [SCENE 3]
14-20s: [SCENE 4, the payoff or the logo]

TEXT ON SCREEN
0.5-3s: "[HEADLINE, 6 words max]"
3.5-8s: "[LINE 2]"
8.5-14s: "[LINE 3]"
14.5-20s: "[FINAL LINE OR BRAND NAME]"
Text style: bold clean sans-serif, big enough to read on a phone, colour [HEX]. Each line fades and slides up in, then fades out. Keep all text between 15% and 85% of the screen height and away from the right edge, where Instagram's buttons sit.

ENDING
[Loop seamlessly so the last frame flows into the first] OR [Play once and hold the final frame for 2 seconds]
The video is exactly [LENGTH] seconds in total; if it holds the final frame, the last 2 seconds are the held final frame.

TECHNICAL RULES (keep these exactly as they are)
1. Vertical 9:16 video. Call renderer.setPixelRatio(1) and renderer.setSize(1080, 1920, false) so the drawing buffer is exactly 1080x1920. Scale the preview to fit the window with CSS only.
2. Load Three.js as an ES module from cdnjs and nothing else: https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/0.180.0/three.module.min.js
3. One single HTML file with the HTML, CSS and JavaScript together. No outside images, 3D models or font files. Build every object from Three.js shapes.
4. Render every text line with a 2D canvas into a CanvasTexture on a plane, either inside the Three.js scene or in a screen-space orthographic overlay scene rendered by the same WebGLRenderer right after the main scene. Use the overlay for captions so they stay flat and sharp. Text materials use toneMapped: false. The canvas you record must be the only canvas and must contain the text.
5. Run all motion from one master timeline clock in seconds, based on real elapsed time, so the animation always lasts exactly as long as planned.
6. Under the video, add a small control bar: Play/Pause, Restart, and a scrubber that shows the current second.
7. Add a "Record MP4" button. It restarts the animation from 0, records the canvas for the full length at 30 fps with the browser's built-in MediaRecorder (MP4 if the browser supports it, otherwise WebM, around 12 Mbps), then downloads the file automatically.
8. Use sRGB output with ACES filmic tone mapping for the 3D objects. Text, logo and background use MeshBasicMaterial (or scene.background) with toneMapped: false so they match my hex codes exactly. Keep it smooth on a normal laptop: pixel ratio stays at 1, shadow map size 1024 or less, shadows only where they really show, reuse geometries and materials.
9. Do not import any Three.js add-ons (no OrbitControls, EffectComposer, bloom, Reflector, loaders). Fake glow with emissive materials plus additive-blended sprites with a radial-gradient CanvasTexture. Fake depth with fog. Fake floor reflections with a mirrored copy of the objects under a semi-transparent floor.
10. Keep the scene 30 seconds or less and the code compact so it fits in one reply.

title: Flat Drawings Turn Into 3D Houses
author: samnang_aing
prompt:

floor plan: [slab, walls, glazing, cladding, rafters, roof]. Ink on pale paper, numbered
labels in a column on the right, and dotted lines from each layer to where it lands.

The scroll, in order:
1. The loader is a plotter. A pen front sweeps up the model from the ground to the roof,
   lines first in amber, then ink, then the fills. The headline slides up.
2. The layers land one by one, in building order. Everything above a layer drops with it.
   The landing layer turns amber and its label lights up.
3. The camera comes down to [the porch]. The lens widens until the drawing becomes a room
   at eye height, and the glass door slides open.
4. The walk: [the dining table, the stove, up the ladder to the loft], with a caption at
   each stop, ending on a view back across the house.

What I care about:
- The axo is not a picture. It is the real 3D model seen through a 1.5 degree lens from
  about a kilometre away. Widening the lens as the camera comes in (a dolly zoom) turns
  it into eye-level perspective.
- Slab, walls and roof float upward. Glazing and cladding slide out sideways from their
  own wall.
- It stays a drawing inside: crease edges as screen-space lines in three weights, pale
  fills with grain drawn in code.
- Inside, the camera stays level, and a small plan in the corner shows where you stand.
- The look: a CAD screen. Paper #f2efe7, ink #1d1c19, one amber accent #e85d04, Chakra
  Petch for headlines, IBM Plex Mono for labels, a thin frame with corner marks.

title: Wind-Grown Physics Sand Dunes
author: KanaWorks_AI
prompt:
Godot 4（Forward+）で、物理で動くリアルな砂漠を作って。計算はGPUのcompute shaderで。
地形は「高さの格子」を3段重ね
・遠景：約1km四方を0.5m格子
・中景：約33m四方を1.6cm格子
・足元：キャラクターに追従する約4m四方を2mm格子
・細かい層の内側では粗い層を描かない（継ぎ目のちらつき防止）

砂丘は描かずに、風で育てる（Werner型モデル）
・512m周期の領域を0.5m格子で、3000ステップ
・毎ステップ：風上の高い所から10〜15°の「風の影」に入っていないマスから砂を少し持ち上げ、約4m風下に落とす
・影の中には必ず積もる。砂の上は積もりやすく、むき出しの地面は積もりにくい
・33°より急な斜面は崩す
・最後に稜線を少し丸め、滑落面を31〜33°に。結果はキャッシュ
足跡と崩れ
・靴底の形で高さを押し下げ、押しのけた分を縁に盛る（体積保存）
・毎フレーム、急すぎる分だけ8近傍へ砂を流す。止まった砂は34°、流れ出したら28°まで崩れる
・湿った砂は崩れにくくする

舞い上がる砂
・削った体積とまったく同じ量を粒子にして飛ばし、着地したら整数アトミックで高さに足し戻す（砂の総量は不変）
・重力＋空気抵抗＋風
・粉塵は3層（濃い芯／外側／長く漂う層）、自己影と地形の影つき
見た目（自作シェーダ）
・法線＝高さ＋波長と向きの違う風紋2つをノイズで混ぜる＋ピクセルサイズの粒の凹凸
・拡散はd'EonのLambert-sphere＋Hapke
・影には空の青い光と、周りの日向からの暖かい照り返し
・きらめき：ワールドに固定した1px未満の点を、太陽と視線のハーフベクトルが風紋の法線に近い所だけ光らせる（太陽側に光の帯ができる）
・セルフシャドウは高さ場のレイマーチ
光とカメラ
・低い太陽（13〜16°）を風下側に置き、稜線で光と影を分ける
・空気遠近の霧を数層
・動画は120fpsで書き出し、4フレームを線形光で平均して30fps（自然なモーションブラー）

On-screen text: [title only / none / lyrics]

title: The Big One Anime Short
author: makerjackie
prompt:
Make me an animated short film entirely in code: no image models, no video models, no audio assets.

[Story] One line: ________ (e.g. a little robot in a straw hat goes fishing, hooks a 220 m ancient whale shark, and gets back the hat the wind blew away)
[Length] about ___ seconds (30-60 works well)
[Look] hand-drawn anime feel: bright summer, deep blue sky, towering cumulus, two-tone cel shading, ink lines, painterly backgrounds (swap for your own style)
[Sound] a score and sound effects, no dialogue
[Reference] you may study https://github.com/0xCodez/leviathan for its render pipeline and modelling approach, but the story and characters must be original

Technical:
1. three.js (WebGL2), bundled with esbuild into one HTML that plays offline; export a 1080p MP4 frame by frame with puppeteer + ffmpeg.
2. Every frame is a pure function of time, renderAt(t): seeded randomness, no accumulated state. During playback the audio clock drives the picture.
3. Pipeline: MRT colour + normal/depth/material id → painterly background pass → ink lines from material id, depth and normal breaks → atmosphere → bloom → grade and grain. Characters use a two-tone cel material.
4. Characters on twos, effects on threes, like hand-drawn animation.
5. Write the shot list first: story cues and shots; a director module returns camera, poses, expressions and effects for any time.
6. Model the main characters and creatures properly: build the real form in a rest pose from section curves plus sculpting (bony ridges, face, fins/limbs, a jaw and eyelids that move), then bend it along a skeleton on the GPU; paint the skin in the shader and break the terminator with bumped normals. No single tube or stack of spheres.
7. Motion must feel alive: anticipation, the head trailing, twisting, follow-through, squash and stretch on landing. Nothing may teleport.
8. Give the sound to a parallel sub-agent: synthesize the score and effects in pure JS against the cue sheet, stereo out.

Quality, every round:

title: Loop Notes App Launch Film
author: TylerMommsen
prompt:
Create a 20 second launch video for a note taking app called Loop, using HyperFrames.


PRODUCT
- Loop is a note taking app for busy people who write notes and never look at them again.
- Promise: your notes come back when you need them.
- Show three features in this order:
  Capture: get a thought down in seconds.
  Connect: related notes link themselves.
  Resurface: old notes come back at the right moment.


STORY
- Hook, three features, logo. You design the scenes and write the words.
- One idea runs through the whole video: a single red line that never leaves the screen.
  It ends as the loop in the logo.
- Every scene must transform into the next one. Nothing fades or cuts. For example
  the logo opens into the app, or a headline melts into the logo.
- No scene may be a headline on the left with a card on the right.
- End on the "loop" wordmark, a short tagline and a small "Available now" label.


FORMAT
- 1920x1080, 16:9, 60 fps, exactly 20 seconds, exported as an MP4.


LOOK
- Premium and calm, like a launch film from a top design studio. Lots of empty space.
- Background #F2EFE9, text #15140F, one accent color only, red #E5432D.
- The final logo scene flips to a dark background, #141413, with a soft red glow.
- Headlines in Instrument Serif. App text in Geist. Small labels in Geist Mono.
- Build the app screens in code so they look like a real, finished product.
- Avoid: gradients, stock icons, more than one accent color, anything that looks like a template.


MOTION
- The camera is always moving slowly. Nothing sits frozen on screen.
- Give it real depth: tilt the app window in 3D, soft shadows, blur on things far away.
- Real motion blur like a film camera: render extra in-between frames and blend them.
- Keep app screens big enough that every word is easy to read.


SOUND
- Make the music and every sound effect in code. No stock files, no samples.
- Soft, warm, minimal music at about 100 beats per minute. Scene changes land on the beat.
- A sound for every action: typing, lines drawing, notes landing, the logo.
- Every sound sits on the exact frame of the thing it belongs to.


QUALITY CHECK
- When the first version is done, render it and look at a frame from every half second.
- Critique it the way a senior motion designer would: story, layout, spacing, type, timing,
  depth, readability, and whether the sound matches the picture.
- Fix everything you find, render again, and critique again.
- Do at least four full rounds before you consider stopping. After each round, write
  down what was weak and what you changed.
- After that, keep going until a full critique finds nothing left to fix and it looks
  perfect and premium, like a senior motion designer made it. There is no limit on rounds.


RULES
- Don't stop and don't ask me anything. Skip any approval steps and make every
  decision yourself.
- When it's finished, give me the final MP4, confirm it has sound, and list what you
  fixed in each round.

title: Blender MCP Mecha Build Timelapse
author: Muska-2026
prompt:
CREATIVE WORKFLOW  /  3D AUTOMATION
HEAVY UTILITY
MECH  M-72
OPUS 5.5  +  BLENDER  /  ANIMATED MECHA
  

BASIC TUTORIAL & LIVE MODELING BRIEF
21 sections  /  Blender MCP  /  OBS timelapse  /  EEVEE  /  Rigging & animation
Tutorial reference  ›  https://youtube.com/shorts/xCkjVUtVDEw?feature=share
________________


1. PRIMARY OBJECTIVE
  

You are an expert 3D hard-surface artist, mechanical designer, technical director, and Blender automation agent operating Blender directly through MCP.
Your mission is to reconstruct the supplied M-72 heavy industrial mecha with exceptional geometric detail, mechanical accuracy, realistic materials, and a fully developed desert environment.
This is not simply a 3D modeling task. It is a live, visually directed modeling performance.
The entire process will be recorded using OBS directly from the Blender interface.
Your actions must create the impression of an experienced professional 3D artist progressively building, inspecting, refining, and presenting an extremely sophisticated mechanical object.
The final deliverables are:
•  A complete, production-quality 3D mecha.
•  Mechanically coherent geometry and articulated components.
•  Highly realistic PBR materials and surface finishes.
•  A realistic desert environment matching the supplied references.
•  Professional lighting and composition using EEVEE exclusively.
•  A functional animation rig.
•  A short final animation where the mecha walks away and exits the camera frame.
•  A visually compelling, continuously observable modeling process, suitable for editing into a social media timelapse.
Prioritize geometric fidelity, craftsmanship, visual clarity, and meaningful visible progression over execution speed.
Do not simplify complex structures merely to complete the project faster.
2. REFERENCE FIDELITY — ABSOLUTE PRIORITY
Use the supplied beauty render and technical concept sheet as primary visual references.
The beauty render establishes:
•  Overall proportions and silhouette.
•  Mecha posture and mass distribution.
•  Armor shapes and major mechanical volumes.
•  Surface appearance and weathering.
•  Materials and overall color palette.
•  Lighting, atmosphere, and desert environment.
The concept sheet establishes:
•  Component organization.
•  Mechanical construction.
•  Joint locations.
•  Cable routing.
•  Hydraulic assemblies.
•  Structural articulation.
•  Connections between armor and internal machinery.
•  Small mechanical details.
Continuously compare the actual model against these references throughout production.
Do not rely on memory or approximate interpretations of the design.
Establish reference images in Blender, preferably using properly positioned reference image objects or a dedicated reference collection.
Create regular visual checkpoints to compare the model from corresponding angles.
When a discrepancy is detected, correct it before continuing to the next major assembly.
Maintain consistency between front, side, rear, and three-quarter views.
If the reference sheet contains contradictory perspectives or mechanically impossible connections, prioritize the principal beauty render, preserve the original design language, and resolve the contradiction with plausible engineering.
The final mech must be immediately recognizable as the supplied M-72 design, not a generic reinterpretation.
3. PROGRESSIVE MODELING — FROM BLOCKING TO MICRODETAILS
Model the mecha progressively, starting from simple geometric masses and refining each individual component through visible stages.
Never create a fully completed complex component in a single invisible operation.
Each major component must visibly evolve through several construction stages.
Stage A — Primary Blocking
Start with basic geometric primitives.
Create:
•  Main armored torso.
•  Upper mechanical sensor assembly.
•  Pelvis and central frame.
•  Shoulder masses.
•  Upper arms.
•  Forearms and hands.
•  Upper legs.
•  Lower legs.
•  Feet.
Establish proportions, silhouette, pose, and relationships between components.
The blocking must remain clean and easy to interpret.
At this stage, do not introduce unnecessary details.
Stage B — Secondary Geometric Construction
Gradually refine the blocking into recognizable mechanical assemblies.
Introduce:
•  Armor panel segmentation.
•  Primary bevels and chamfers.
•  Recessed surfaces.
•  Structural frames.
•  Large articulation housings.
•  Motor assemblies.
•  Mechanical supports.
•  Hydraulic cylinders.
•  Major ventilation openings.
•  Maintenance panels.
Each primitive must evolve visibly into a sophisticated hard-surface object.
The viewer should understand where every finished structure originated.
Stage C — Mechanical Refinement
Develop the internal engineering.
Add:
•  Rotary bearings.
•  Servo motors.
•  Gearbox housings.
•  Hydraulic actuators.
•  Pistons and rods.
•  Structural brackets.
•  Hinges and pivot mechanisms.
•  Suspension assemblies.
•  Flexible couplings.
•  Mechanical linkage systems.
•  Actuator attachment points.
Mechanisms must have believable construction and motion ranges.
An actuator must connect real mechanical endpoints.
A hydraulic piston must follow the correct mechanical axis and account for articulation.
Avoid decorative mechanical components with no structural or functional purpose.
Stage D — Tertiary Details
Add increasingly fine detail:
•  Individual bolts and fasteners.
•  Machined collars.
•  Threaded elements.
•  Retaining rings.
•  Protective covers.
•  Cable glands.
•  Connectors.
•  Hose couplings.
•  Cooling fins.
•  Access hatches.
•  Mechanical stops.
•  Small reinforcement plates.
•  Grilles and ventilation structures.
•  Surface panel transitions.
Use distinct levels of geometric density to establish a readable visual hierarchy.
Stage E — Microdetails
Finish with high-resolution industrial details:
•  Fine panel seams.
•  Mechanical grooves.
•  Small welds.
•  Precision fasteners.
•  Small mounting rails.
•  Cable clamps.
•  Surface engravings.
•  Warning markings.
•  Identification decals.
•  Fine material transitions.
•  Localized scratches and worn edges.
Small details should reinforce the mechanical design rather than produce meaningless noise.
Every level of refinement must be visibly demonstrated in the viewport.
4. COMPONENT-BY-COMPONENT CONSTRUCTION
Work systematically through the mecha, maintaining a clear assembly hierarchy.
Recommended sequence:
•  Main torso structural frame.
•  Main torso armor and panel construction.
•  Upper optical and sensor module.
•  Shoulder rotary assemblies.
•  Upper arm mechanical structures.
•  Elbow joints and hydraulic actuators.
•  Forearm assemblies.
•  Articulated mechanical hands and fingers.
•  Pelvis and hip structure.
•  Hip rotation mechanisms.
•  Upper leg armor and internal frames.
•  Knee mechanisms.
•  Lower leg actuators and suspension.
•  Ankles and articulated feet.
•  Primary cable networks.
•  Secondary hoses and electrical systems.
•  Connectors, clamps, and fittings.
•  Surface microdetails.
•  Materials, wear, and environmental integration.
For each component:
•  Begin with a visible simple shape or set of primitives.
•  Develop its main geometry.
•  Introduce structural subdivision.
•  Add mechanical details.
•  Inspect the result from useful angles.
•  Refine the topology.
•  Apply appropriate bevel treatments.
•  Add secondary and tertiary details.
•  Assign its primary materials.
•  Verify visual consistency with the references.
•  Integrate it into the larger assembly.
Do not jump randomly between unrelated areas unless required for mechanical dependencies.
Critical Visibility Requirement
Do not hide large amounts of modeling activity inside a single script execution.
Even when using Python to generate geometry, divide the process into meaningful construction operations.
Execute them sequentially and update the Blender viewport between milestones.
Create enough visible intermediate stages for the recorded footage to communicate how the object is actually constructed.
A finished component appearing instantly is not acceptable when it could reasonably be built through several visible stages.
5. VIEWPORT CAMERA — INTELLIGENT ARTIST-LIKE NAVIGATION
This section is essential and has the highest priority for the recording experience.
The Blender viewport must behave as though an experienced 3D artist is actively manipulating the scene while modeling.
The viewport is not a cinematic camera performing a predetermined animation.
It is an intelligent working viewpoint driven by actual modeling activity.
Fundamental Rule
The viewport moves only when a change of viewpoint provides useful visual information about the active modeling operation.
No continuous orbit.
No automatic turnaround.
No idle camera animation.
No repetitive oscillation.
No unnecessary camera resets.
No decorative camera movement.
When Geometry is Actively Changing
Use purposeful viewport navigation to reveal the operation.
Possible actions include:
•  Orbiting around the active component.
•  Slightly rotating to reveal a newly created surface.
•  Zooming in to inspect a joint or bevel.
•  Zooming out to evaluate proportions.
•  Panning to a neighboring assembly.
•  Moving to a side view to inspect actuator alignment.
•  Moving above or below a component to inspect hidden connections.
Select the viewing angle according to the operation.
Examples:
When constructing a cylinder, move to an angle where its axial geometry and surface refinement are readable.
When creating a recessed armor panel, choose an angle that clearly reveals its depth.
When adjusting a hydraulic piston, choose a viewpoint where its attachment points and stroke direction are visible.
When routing cables, move to reveal their origin, destination, and path around obstacles.
When working on a complex shoulder joint, use short deliberate orbit movements to reveal the mechanical layers.
When No Modeling Activity is Occurring
Stop all viewport movement immediately.
Maintain the last useful viewing position.
Do not return to a predefined viewpoint.
Do not reset the camera.
Do not rotate to fill idle time.
Do not perform a turnaround.
Do not introduce artificial movement while processing scripts or waiting for operations to finish.
The last camera position becomes the starting point for the next meaningful navigation action.
Navigation Continuity
Treat viewport navigation as a continuous sequence of artist decisions.
Each movement should begin from the current viewport orientation and position.
Never automatically return to the initial three-quarter angle between operations.
When moving from one component to another:
•  Identify the new component.
•  Determine the most useful viewing angle.
•  Transition smoothly from the current viewpoint.
•  Recenter on the active area.
•  Adjust zoom to show the relevant geometry.
•  Stop once an effective working view is reached.
Do not orbit unnecessarily around the entire mecha to reach the destination.
Use the shortest visually coherent navigation.
Movement Style
Navigation must feel:
•  Deliberate.
•  Fluid.
•  Responsive.
•  Technical.
•  Precise.
•  Natural.
•  Efficient.
Avoid mechanical, repetitive camera motion.
Use restrained easing when transitioning between views.
Do not interpolate constantly during extended modeling operations if a static view is more informative.
A stationary viewport while geometry evolves is often more visually satisfying than a moving viewport.
6. VIEWPORT FRAMING AND SOCIAL MEDIA COMPOSITION
The Blender application will be recorded through OBS.
Maintain the viewport as the dominant visible working area.
Maximize the 3D Viewport whenever practical.
Avoid unnecessary interface panels occupying a substantial portion of the recording.
The mecha or currently edited component must remain clearly visible.
The framing must be suitable for cropping into social media formats.
Prioritize a central safe composition suitable for:
•  Instagram Reels.
•  TikTok.
•  YouTube Shorts.
•  Vertical 9:16 editing.
Even if the OBS recording is made in a wider format, keep the active subject and its essential construction details within a central region whenever practical.
Use different framing scales according to the operation:
Wide framing: overall structure, proportions, major assemblies, and full-body inspections.
Medium framing: torso, shoulder, leg, and arm construction.
Close-up framing: pistons, rotational joints, cable connectors, fasteners, and individual mechanical elements.
Extreme close-up: precision surface refinement and small geometric details.
Never zoom so far into an object that the viewer loses all understanding of the assembly being constructed.
Maintain sufficient surrounding context.
Do not allow important modifications to occur outside the visible viewport.
Avoid clipping the active object against the viewport borders.
7. SHOW THE ACTUAL MODELING PROCESS
The objective is not simply to display successive model states.
The recording should show recognizable Blender modeling operations whenever practical.
Examples include:
•  Transforming primitives.
•  Extruding faces.
•  Insetting surfaces.
•  Applying bevels.
•  Creating mechanical cutouts.
•  Adding modifiers.
•  Building structural components.
•  Editing mesh profiles.
•  Creating curves for hoses.
•  Converting mechanical profiles into finished structures.
•  Duplicating and assembling repeated parts.
•  Adjusting origins and pivot locations.
•  Connecting objects into mechanical assemblies.
Favor a construction rhythm where the viewer can clearly perceive the change between successive stages.
When using procedural modeling or Python-generated geometry, progressively expose the underlying construction.
For example, a sophisticated mechanical joint should not immediately appear as a finished object.
Instead show:
•  Basic cylinder.
•  Structural housing.
•  Inner bearing assembly.
•  Outer reinforcement rings.
•  Fasteners.
•  Hydraulic mounting points.
•  Surface detailing.
•  Material refinement.
Make the transformation from simple primitives to complex mechanical assemblies visually satisfying.
Do not deliberately slow down computations unnecessarily, but avoid batching unrelated construction stages into an invisible operation.
8. MECHANICAL ENGINEERING AND GEOMETRY REQUIREMENTS
Treat the mecha as a credible piece of heavy industrial machinery.
Its external appearance must reflect a coherent underlying mechanical structure.
Joint Construction
Every major joint requires:
•  A clearly identifiable rotational or translational axis.
•  A structural load-bearing connection.
•  Appropriate mechanical clearance.
•  Actuator connections.
•  Protective elements.
•  Mechanical travel limits.
•  Cable or hydraulic routing consistent with the intended movement.
Do not create floating actuators or disconnected mechanical components.
Cable and Hose Networks
The original design contains numerous complex cable assemblies.
Reconstruct these carefully.
Distinguish between:
•  Electrical cable bundles.
•  Hydraulic hoses.
•  Data cables.
•  Protective conduits.
•  Cooling pipes.
•  Rigid hydraulic tubing.
Each cable must have a logical origin, destination, routing path, and attachment system.
Use Blender curves with controlled bevel profiles or suitable procedural geometry.
Create:
•  Cable clamps.
•  Fastening brackets.
•  Connection sockets.
•  Couplings.
•  Protective sleeves.
•  Retaining rings.
•  Cable management channels.
Avoid arbitrary floating cables.
Avoid cables passing through armor.
Avoid unnecessary cable intersections.
Maintain appropriate slack at articulated joints.
Cables crossing joints must account for expected movement and should not become unrealistically stretched during animation.
Armor Construction
Armor must be designed as physically plausible individual panels.
Use actual dimensional thickness where visually necessary.
Avoid infinitely thin structural components.
Keep consistent panel gaps and assembly clearances.
Armor should follow underlying structural logic rather than merely imitate surface patterns.
9. TOPOLOGY, BEVELS, AND MESH QUALITY
Maintain professional geometric quality throughout the entire project.
Avoid:
•  Unintended coplanar overlapping faces.
•  Duplicate faces.
•  Z-fighting.
•  Degenerate polygons.
•  Invalid normals.
•  Unnecessary internal geometry.
•  Visible Boolean artifacts.
•  Broken shading.
•  Accidental mesh intersections.
•  Inconsistent bevel widths.
•  Overlapping mechanical assemblies.
•  Unintended self-intersecting bevels.
Use appropriate geometry tools such as:
•  Bevel modifiers.
•  Weighted normals or compatible normal-control workflows.
•  Boolean operations.
•  Array modifiers.
•  Mirror modifiers.
•  Subdivision where appropriate.
•  Custom mesh construction.
Use Clamp Overlap when appropriate for bevel operations.
Apply carefully chosen bevel widths relative to local geometric scale.
Do not allow bevels to collapse narrow surfaces or intersect adjacent details.
Inspect bevel behavior around complex corners and thin armor sections.
Use angle-limited or weight-controlled bevels when they provide better results.
Apply object scale appropriately before operations that depend on geometric dimensions.
Keep shading consistent across hard-surface transitions.
Check geometry quality after major Boolean or bevel operations.
Run mesh integrity checks at logical milestones.
No visible topology defect should remain in the finished model.
10. ULTRA-REALISTIC MATERIALS AND TEXTURES
Build physically credible materials using a professional PBR workflow.
The primary surfaces should include:
Armored Steel
•  Desaturated sandy beige.
•  Slightly irregular paint.
•  Subtle roughness variation.
•  Edge wear and chipped coatings.
•  Exposed metal along selected damaged edges.
•  Embedded desert dust.
Dark Mechanical Steel
•  Graphite and gunmetal finishes.
•  Machined metal surfaces.
•  Distinct brushed-metal variation.
•  Subtle oxidation and grime.
•  Oil accumulation near working joints.
Hydraulic Components
•  Metallic rods with controlled reflections.
•  Dark actuator housings.
•  Seals and protective collars.
•  Machined attachment brackets.
•  Localized grease or oil around moving parts.
Rubber and Composite Elements
•  Matte black cable coatings.
•  Slight micro-surface texture.
•  Different roughness values for protective sleeves and flexible hoses.
•  Subtle accumulated dust.
Yellow Industrial Markings
•  Weathered warning stripes.
•  Chipped paint.
•  Faded industrial identification.
•  Small safety markings.
Use geometry and high-resolution textures together.
Textures should enhance existing structural detail, not substitute for mechanical geometry.
Apply suitable UV mapping and consistent texel density.
Use high-resolution roughness, metallic, normal, and optional displacement-style detail where beneficial and compatible with EEVEE.
Use texture assets where appropriate, including high-quality external resources if available.
If suitable assets cannot be obtained, create sophisticated procedural materials rather than defaulting to flat colors.
Avoid excessive scratches or random grunge.
Weathering must follow believable patterns of mechanical use and environmental exposure.
11. DESERT ENVIRONMENT
Reconstruct the environment seen in the reference beauty render.
The mech stands in a realistic, open, arid desert landscape.
Create:
•  Sandy terrain with realistic surface variation.
•  Fine gravel and small stones.
•  Subtle dry soil textures.
•  Sparse desert vegetation.
•  Dust accumulation around the feet.
•  Distant atmospheric haze.
•  Pale blue desert sky.
•  Subtle warm atmospheric perspective.
Match the overall visual character of the original reference.
Use a restrained environment composition.
The mech must remain the dominant subject.
Avoid excessive environmental props that distract from its geometry.
Introduce realistic terrain contact beneath the feet.
Ensure the mecha feels heavy and physically connected to the ground.
The final environment must not resemble a generic procedural plane.
12. EEVEE-ONLY RENDERING AND LIGHTING
Use Blender EEVEE exclusively.
Do not switch to Cycles.
Do not launch final offline renders.
Do not execute unnecessary render operations.
All artistic evaluation must occur through the Blender viewport.
Use Material Preview or Rendered viewport shading as appropriate, with the final visual appearance evaluated in EEVEE.
Optimize the scene for responsive viewport interaction without sacrificing the final level of detail.
Develop professional daylight illumination featuring:

STYLE GUIDE: "Paper-Cutout Storybook Collage"
1. The look in one sentence
A hand-made paper collage in a children's-storybook style. Every character and prop is a watercolor and colored-pencil illustration cut out of paper, with a thin white die-cut border and a soft drop shadow. The cutouts are layered flat on textured paper backgrounds: cream watercolor paper, kraft cardboard, watercolor washes and torn-paper strips. Motion is snappy and playful, like stop-motion, with ransom-note typography, hand-lettered captions and pencil doodles.
2. Materials and surfaces
* Cutouts:
   * Each character or prop is a separate watercolor and colored-pencil painting. It shows paper grain, soft pigment blooms and loose pencil outlines.
   * Every cutout has a clean white paper border (about 6–12 px at 1080p) following its silhouette, like a die-cut sticker.
   * Underneath is a soft, warm drop shadow: roughly 0 9px 7px rgba(74,48,22,0.30) layered with a tight 0 2px 1.5px rgba(0,0,0,0.20).
* Full-frame backgrounds (rotate between these):
   * Cream cold-press watercolor paper with faint fibers, a soft warm vignette, and a few faint pencil sparkle doodles in the corners.
   * Brown kraft cardboard or handmade fibrous paper with flecks, used like a pinboard for taped "photos" and paper tags.
   * Watercolor skies:
      * pale blue and cream with loose painted clouds;
      * deep navy night with white splatter-paint stars;
      * gloomy charcoal soot for somber moments;
      * warm amber for dramatic moments.
   * Landscapes built from layered torn-paper strips (hills, ground, sea), each with ragged white torn-fiber edges and a slight shadow between layers.
* Craft-table props:
   * washi-tape strips (pink, mustard or teal, semi-transparent) holding photos and tags;
   * cream paper tags and labels;
   * polaroid-style photo cards with thick bottom borders;
   * paper confetti squares and torn paper scraps.
* Everything is flat and seen head-on, like a paper diorama photographed straight on. Avoid 3D rendering, glossy gradients, photorealism, and heavy blur or glow.
3. Color palette
* Tomato red #d9483b
* Mustard #e0a73a
* Teal #2f7f7a
* Ultramarine #2f4fa8
* Olive #7c8a3c
* Sage #9dbb8e
* Blush pink #f1a9a0
* Cream #f3ecdf
* Paper white #fbf7ee
* Kraft #b98f5e
* Ink #2b2622
* Pencil #3a332c
* Night navy #1b2a4a
The overall feel is warm and muted, like gouache or watercolor on paper. Saturation is gentle; the brightest accents are tomato red and mustard.
4. Character design
* Cute, round, chunky proportions with big heads.
* Small solid black dot eyes, simple curved smiles, and rosy blush circles on the cheeks.
* Soft watercolor fills with darker pencil outlines.
* Animals and creatures follow the same rules. They are friendly and slightly comic, never scary, even in dramatic moments. For example, a panicked T. rex yells with little sweat drops, and a sad dinosaur shivers with an icicle on its nose.
* Objects can have faces when it's funny: a mischievous asteroid, a surprised wave, a sleepy sun, a worried bullet.
* Use one recurring hero character with a signature outfit, such as a small kid in a red beanie and yellow raincoat, or a curly-haired kid in a blue knitted sweater.
   * Keep them identical across shots by using an earlier image of them as a reference.
   * Make pose variants of the same character: pointing, crying, cheering, waving.
5. Typography (only three kinds of text)
1. Ransom-note titles:
   * Each letter sits on its own small paper square, and each square has a different color and font.
   * Tiles get a slight random rotation (about ±6°), some vertical jitter and a small drop shadow; some letters are lowercase.
   * Tile styles:
      * black with cream or mustard letters;
      * cream with red or black letters;
      * red with cream letters;
      * ultramarine with mustard letters;
      * mustard with black letters;
      * pink with dark red or blue letters;
      * a red polka-dot tile;
      * a blue grid-paper tile;
      * teal with cream letters.
   * Mixed display fonts: Alfa Slab One, Abril Fatface, Bowlby One, Special Elite, Bungee, Titan One, Ultra, Lilita One, Bebas Neue, Playfair Display Black, Rubik Mono One.
   * Letters slap on one at a time (about 0.04–0.05 s apart), synced to the spoken words.
2. Hand-lettered brush captions:
   * Set in "Caveat Brush" in dark ink #2b2622.
   * Revealed letter by letter like handwriting.
   * Often followed by a red pencil double underline that draws itself on in two slightly wobbly strokes.
3. Small labels:
   * Set in "Patrick Hand" on cream paper tags held by a strip of washi tape.
   * Sometimes a red pencil check mark or circle draws on next to them.
On-screen text stays short: a title, a number or a punchline word, never full narration sentences. Keep text about 90 px from the frame edges.
6. Pencil doodles
* Drawn in ink #3a332c, 3–5 px wide, with round caps.
* Types:
   * sparkle crosses in corners;
   * "?" and "!" above characters;
   * speed lines, impact ticks and motion arcs;
   * dashed travel trails;
   * "z z z" and shiver marks.
* They draw themselves on as strokes, or pop in and wobble.
7. Composition
* 16:9 at 1920×1080, 30 fps.
* Flat, straight-on camera, generous negative space, one clear idea per frame.
* Build depth by layering: background → torn-paper middle layers → props → characters → a foreground strip (hills or ferns) that characters can pop up from behind.
* A subtle warm vignette over everything.
* Recurring layouts:
   * a character bottom-left looking up at a ransom-note title;
   * photos taped to a kraft board;
   * a row of objects appearing one per word;
   * a big central prop with small tags around it.
8. Motion language (JavaScript / GSAP)
* Pop-in with overshoot: from scale 0 and about ±12° rotation up to full size with back.out(2–3), pivoting at the bottom (the feet).
* Drop-in from above with a bounce, slide-in from off-frame, and hops with squash and stretch from the feet.
* Never frozen: everything on screen gets a gentle idle sway or bob (±1.5–4° rotation, a few pixels), with a finite number of repeats.
* Stop-motion boil: stepped random jitter at 8–10 fps for shivering, nerves, crying, fire flicker and shaking ground.
* Signature gags:
   * crowds or objects multiply (1 → 2 → 4 → 8 …);
   * things tear in half along matching jagged edges, and the halves fall away with scraps;
   * a paper-flip swap turns one thing into another: scaleX 1 → 0, swap the image, 0 → 1, with a puff of paper confetti;
   * things shrink in squashy steps;
   * photos get taped onto a board.
* Camera:
   * slow push-ins (scale 1 → about 1.03–1.04 over a scene);
   * stepped shakes on impacts;
   * occasional pans between stacked layers.
* Sync rule:
   * Every reveal lands on, or about 0.05 s before, the exact spoken word it illustrates.
   * One sentence equals one visual beat.
   * Never put everything on screen at once; reveal it across the scene.
* Snappy and playful: anticipation → action → follow-through. Never floaty, never corporate, no linear motion.
* For reliable rendering, use only seeded randomness, only finite repeats, and a timeline that can jump to any frame.
9. Scene transitions
* Default: a new full-frame paper sheet slides over the previous scene from one side.
   * It takes 0.5–0.7 s with power3.out and settles from a slight rotation.
   * Its torn leading edge shows white paper fibers, with a drop shadow.
   * Vary the direction each scene: right, left, top, bottom.
* Variations:
   * a heavy dark sheet dropping from the top for somber beats (power2.inOut, about 0.9 s, small settle bounce);
   * a fast whip (about 0.4 s, expo.out) for urgency;
   * a white flash or bloom for explosions.
* Start each incoming sheet about 0.3 s after the previous line's last word so the punchline lands.
* No exit animations: the next sheet is the exit.
10. Writing style of the narration
* Tone: a warm, wry, gentle storybook narrator. Dry understatement, never snarky or mean. Speaks inclusively ("we", "you").
* Hook: open with a big question, which also appears on screen as the ransom-note title.
* Sentences:
   * Short (about 5–9 words) and lots of fragments.
   * Lots of periods, with pauses after punchlines.
   * Conversational asides ("for, well, forever").
* Rule of three with a deflating third beat: two straight items, then a deadpan comic one. Example: "Philosophers wrote enormous books. The stars kept quiet. And the cat said: 'Nap.'"
* Facts:
   * Deliver them as concrete images and comparisons, not a pile of statistics.
   * Use at most one number per sentence ("a rock the size of Mount Everest").
   * Use lists of short sensory fragments.
* Ending: a turn near the end ("Turns out…" or "But…"), then a warm, witty closing line or instruction that ties back to the opening question.
* Every sentence must work as one visual gag.
* Pacing: the original style is slow, about 110 words per minute of video. If the script is 140–160 words, shorten the long pauses after recording so the video stays near 60 seconds.
11. Sound
* Music:
   * A whimsical storybook track: pizzicato strings, ukulele, glockenspiel, soft clarinet and light brushed percussion, about 100 BPM, instrumental.
   * It sits about 15–20 dB under the voice.
   * Turn it down or muffle it (low-pass) for somber moments; let it swell slightly on the end card.
* Paper-craft sound effects, kept subtle:
   * soft paper swishes for sheet transitions;
   * light taps for ransom letters;
   * cartoon pops when cutouts appear;
   * a boing for hops;
   * a paper-tear sound when things tear;
   * a thud for drops;
   * a sparkle chime for magic moments.
* Bigger booms and rumbles only for real drama.
* Final loudness: about −14 LUFS, with peaks below −1.5 dBFS.
12. Generating the image elements (Higgsfield, GPT Image 2.5)
* Cutouts (transparent background, 2K, high quality). Prompt template:
"Paper-cutout sticker asset for a stop-motion collage animation, on a FULLY TRANSPARENT background. Hand-painted watercolor + colored-pencil children's-storybook illustration, cut out of watercolor paper with a thin clean white paper border following the whole silhouette (die-cut sticker edge). Single isolated object, centered, whole object visible with generous margin, flat straight-on view, no cast shadow, no ground, no scenery, no text. Palette: tomato red, mustard yellow, teal, ultramarine, olive, sage green, blush pink, cream. Cute round design, small black dot eyes, rosy blush cheeks. Match the character designs and art style of the attached storyboard sheet. SUBJECT: …"
   * Attach the approved storyboard grid, or an earlier character cutout, as an image reference for consistency.
   * Trim the transparent margins before use.
   * Backgrounds (opaque, 16:9):
   * blank textured cream watercolor paper;
   * blank kraft cardboard;
   * watercolor skies with layered torn-paper hills (no characters);
   * navy starry night with white splatter stars;
   * sooty charcoal sky with a torn-paper ground strip.
   * Storyboard grid: one 16:9 image with 3×3 panels, thin cream gutters, and a small number tag on each panel. Describe each panel in order, all in the style above.
   * Built in code, not generated as images (HTML/CSS/SVG):
   * ransom letters, captions and tags;
   * washi tape, confetti and doodles;
   * underlines;
   * screens and simple interface elements.
